note: The field journal (docs 13, 15): the words it writes and the numbers that shape them. order: the living things with pages, in page order. Each species: name and icon (src/ui/icons), riddle (shown before it has been seen), amount ([at least this many plants, words] steps; a cover plant (kind cover: grass, rushes) uses its share of the dry ground instead, or with amountBy area the square meters it covers), place and compass (where words: compass false skips the side of the island), none (after it has gone), clause words (flowering, dormant, spreading, receding), stages (what tapping one says, by growth stage: seed, sprout, young, mature, flowering, dormant), seasons (what each season box says: grow per season, flower, dormant), likes (lines learned when one of the learn triggers happens: seen, spread, flower, lost:drown, lost:seed, refused:<need>, grass:flooded), gives (a pencil line until the when trigger, then the ink line), notes (the lines the journal writes). trend: a species is spreading when it has gained at least max(upMin, upShare x then) plants over trend hours, receding when it has lost at least max(downMin, downShare x then). where: spreadOut is the mean distance from the plants' middle, as a share of the island's radius, past which they are all around the island; centerShare is how close to the island's middle counts as the middle. notesKept: notes the journal keeps; pageNotes: notes on a species page. islandNote: how long a note stays on the island (showS), the gap between two (gapS) and how many may wait (queue). identify: how near a tap must be to a plant (radiusM), how long the card stays (showS; it closes by itself only after closeS at the least, never while the pointer is over it or after one of its actions was pressed, and for closingGraceS after closing it still takes a late press so it never falls through as a walk), and the size of the breathing ring around what was tapped (ringM for a full-grown plant, smaller for young ones; grassRingM on grass; its timing is in recipes/world/growth.json marks); a species may set its own tapM (how near a tap must be) and ringM, as grey willow does for its wide crown. arrivedHours: plants seen within this many hours of the journal starting were here when you arrived. J1.5: each species also has plural (for the story lines), field (field notes: natural history lines learned like likes, by triggers that include dormant, woke and moment:<id>) and fieldHint (the pencil line while some are still to learn). story: the lines of 'your island's story' ({Plural}, {plural} and {date} are filled in; peak shows when the count has fallen under peakShare of its best). moments: four frames per page by kind (plant, cover for grass and rushes, ground in journal-island.json), each filled the first time you tap that thing at that moment: flower (in flower), summer, winter, rain (rain at least rainAt), mist (at least mistAt), dawn and dusk (hours of the day, inclusive start, exclusive end), frost (a winter dawn); note is the line written. showMe: how long (showS) the ring and card stay after a page's Show me rings the example nearest the middle of your view (the camera does not move). S6a, animals: a creature (kind creature: frogs) is known only once you find one yourself (tap it, or watch it from close by; recipes/species/frog.json find), never just because it is on the island; until then its page shows the riddle, or the latest of its hints whose journal flag is set (frogs:right when the pond is right for them, frogs:sign after the first sign). Its notes come in two voices: the unseen ones speak of something (a sign, rings on the water), never naming it; the others once it is known. A swarm (kind swarm: midges) is known by itself, like a plant, at the first dusk (seenAt.hours) that at least seenAt.m2 square meters hold seenAt.share of a full cloud; its amount is in those square meters. seenAt.drawn: whether the island draws the swarm yet; until it does (S6b), midges stay a pencil ? and nothing names them, because the journal only tells what you could see. card: what a tap on one says. foundLine: its story's first line. The animals' moments are moments.creature. buried (src/world/journal/buried.js, docs/future/13 PR-21, PR-29): line, the kind journal line for a patch still gone an hour after the stroke ({where}: the side of the island and the page's place); stroke, the island's notice when one stroke covers growth.json bury.strokeNotice gather plants ({others}: otherOne or others with numbers, {back}: it or them); session, the notice once a session (load or rest to the next rest) at bury.sessionNotice; showS, how long a notice shows.

grass.name: Grass

field.text: Grass grows from the base of each blade, so it recovers quickly when it is grazed or trodden.
Its roots need air: standing water drowns them in a day or two.
Rain soaks into a meadow instead of running off, because the roots hold the soil open.
On cold dawns, frost whitens the tip of every blade.
By the water grass grows tall and dark; on the dry rise it is shorter and cures to straw in late summer.

rushes.name: Rushes and sedges

field.text: Rushes and sedges are grass-like plants of wet ground. They grow in tight tussocks.
In summer small brown flower tufts sprout near the top of the stems.
Their stems are full of soft pith, which carries air down to roots in the soaked mud.
The stems stay standing through winter, brown at the tips, and frost silvers them at dawn.
In the low light of dusk the sedges show their edges: a sedge's stem is three-sided, a rush's is round.

One clump becomes many: new shoots rise from roots creeping under the mud.
Each brown head is packed with thousands of tiny seeds, every one with its own fluff to fly on.
In winter the dry stalks stand on, and small creatures shelter among them from the wind.
Rain runs down the blades and into the mud around their feet.

Raindrops bead and roll on the waxy pads without wetting them.
In winter they rest as thick roots in the mud, waiting for the water to warm.
Shade from the pads keeps the water beneath them cool.

willow.name: Grey willow

field.text: It is also called sallow. Its leaves are grey-green above and soft, grey and felted beneath.
Its catkins open before its leaves, silky and silver. Each bush is male or female: the males' catkins turn yellow with pollen, the females' turn green.
In early summer its tiny seeds drift off on white fluff, and take only on bare, wet ground.
In winter it stands bare, its young twigs red-brown, each bud pressed flat to the twig under a single scale.
Moths come to the catkins at dusk, early in the year when little else is in flower.

gorse.name: Gorse

field.text: Also called furze or whin. Its leaves are stiff green spines, so the whole bush is a mound of needles that nothing grazes.
Its yellow pea flowers smell of coconut on a warm day, thickest from midwinter into spring.
In hot summer weather its black pods crack open with a snap you can hear, and throw the seeds a few meters.
It flowers in every month of the year. An old saying goes: when gorse is out of blossom, kissing is out of fashion.
Frost browns the tips of its spines, but the mound stays green underneath.

Bees and butterflies work the flower heads on a warm afternoon.
In winter it dies back to a few dark leaves at the water line.

It hunts slugs and small snails in the damp under the log.
If something catches its tail, the tail breaks off and wriggles while the slow worm gets away.

field.text: A woodlouse is not an insect. It is a crustacean, a land cousin of the crabs and shrimps on the shore.
Its shell lets water out easily, so it keeps to the damp and comes out only at night or in the rain.
Woodlice eat dead wood and fallen leaves, and turn them back into soil, as the fungi do.
A mother carries her eggs in a pouch of water under her body, and the young walk out tiny and pale.

field.text: A damselfly folds its wings back along its body when it rests; a dragonfly holds its wings out flat.

Pairs fly joined nose to tail, and the female lays her eggs into stems just under the water.
On cool or wet days they cling low on the stems and hardly fly at all.
Their young live in the pond for about a year, breathing through three leaf-like gills at the tail, then climb a stem to fly.

turtles.name: European pond turtles
turtles._school: A few at a time (M2, src/world/creatures/swarms.js; bask.js), known only once you find one yourself, by tapping it or watching it closely. They come only once summer has warmed the water, need a stone or log at the water's edge to bask on, and sleep in the pond mud from mid-autumn. Their gift is the floating reed raft.
turtles.riddle: Something might come to bask in the sun at a warm pond in summer, if it had somewhere to climb out.

hints.text: Something seems to want warm, still water with lilies, and a stone or log at the edge to climb out on. The pond looks right for it now.
Something dark sat on a stone by the pond this morning, and slid into the water as you looked. Look for it again in the late morning sun.

field.text: A turtle climbs out to bask in the sun: it cannot make its own warmth, so it borrows the sun's.
When spots are few they pile up, one on another's back.
At the first fright they slide off together into the water, and stay under a while.
They eat water plants, and the odd snail or worm.
They sleep the winter in the mud at the bottom of the pond.
A pond turtle can live longer than a person.
